newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq ignores Kuwait elections, celebrates "martyr".
newsitem.headline: Iraq ignores Kuwait elections, celebrates "martyr".

text.p: Iraq studiously ignored elections on Monday in Kuwait, the oil emirate it invaded in 1990 and occupied for seven months.

Government newspapers avoided reference to the parliamentary elections, marking instead the 37th anniversary of a failed assassination attempt against Iraq's military leader Abdul-Karim Qassem in 1959.
They hailed the attack, in which a young Baath Party activist called Saddam Hussein was said to have been injured, as a heroic strike against the "Qassem dictatorship".
Officials on Monday closed off the old pillared Rasheed Street in central Baghdad where the attack took place, erecting a tent in the middle of the road for the commemoration.
A picture of President Saddam Hussein was placed by a statue honouring one of the "martyred" hit men.
"This is the happiest day of the year in Iraq's history," said Muhya al-Qaysi, a retired state employee. "It marks the end of dictatorship."

"The president took part. That's why it's important," said another onlooker who asked not to be named. Qassem escaped the attack unscathed, but was overthrown four years later by an alliance between the Baath Party and army officers.

Most people, questioned about the elections in Kuwait, declined to speak. Some shuffled their feet uncomfortably and looked at the ground when asked about their southern neighbour, which Iraq invaded in 1990 and annexed as its 19th province.
Iraqi troops were evicted from Kuwait in 1991 by a U.S.-led military coalition. Since then Baghdad has formally recognised Kuwait's international borders.
"It's far from us," said Jabbar Abbas. "We're only concerned for our own country."

"The elections in Kuwait should be really democratic, and led by the people of Kuwait, not by outside powers," said history teacher Bahija Hassan, who brought her class of secondary school students to watch the anniversary proceedings.
Kuwait's electorate is tightly restricted to men with proven family history in the emirate going back decades. Women are not allowed to vote.
Analysts in Kuwait said on Monday most voters would be focusing on the emirate's security concerns, which have made it reliant on U.S. armour to reinforce its borders.

They said last month's tension between Washington and Baghdad, which followed Iraq's military intervention to support a rebel Kurdish faction against its rivals, and an Iraqi military buildup on the border with Kuwait in 1994 had heightened Kuwait's sense of vulnerability.

Iraq's own parliamentary elections in March, dominated by concern over the crippling effects of six years of trade sanctions on Baghdad, elected all 160 Baath Party candidates who stood for seats in the 250-seat assembly.
A referendum last October confirmed Saddam in power for seven more years after he won more than 99 percent of the votes.
